title: Does the Voice Change the Grade? A Causal Audit of Speaker-Identity Bias in Audio-LLM Judges
summary: The paper asks whether an audio-input LLM acting as a grader changes the score it assigns to a spoken answer when only the speaker's voice changes and the words are held identical. The authors author 24 interview-style answers once, render each in four accents (American, British, Indian, Nigerian) and two TTS genders, and have three judges (Gemini 3.1 Pro, Gemini 3.6 Flash, Qwen2-Audio-7B) score every clip on a 0-100 rubric, blind to the study purpose. Gemini 3.1 Pro scores Indian-accented renderings 2.50 points lower than the gender-matched American rendering of the same item (95% CI [-4.06, -0.94], p=0.005, d_z=-0.44), Gemini 3.6 Flash shows no effect (-0.04, p=1.00), and Qwen2-Audio-7B scores every non-American accent higher (+1.98 to +2.92). A decomposition arm regrades the same content from the judge's own transcript (+1.88) and from the frozen gold transcript (-0.83), and an explicit interaction test shows the audio-mode shift differs from the own-transcript shift by -6.04 points (p=4e-4). A second axis of five delivery perturbations (filled pauses, speed, 8kHz codec, pink noise) produces no significant shift under either Gemini judge, which the authors report as inconclusive at this sample size rather than as a null result.
central_claim: When an audio-LLM grades a spoken answer, the assigned content score can move with the speaker's voice even though the words are identical, and for the one judge-accent cell where this happens the penalty lives in the acoustic channel and disappears when the same content is graded from a transcript.
strengths: The core design is genuinely causal and correctly executed: text is frozen by construction, the unit of analysis is the within-item, gender-matched paired difference against the American rendering, so item difficulty and gender can never confound the accent contrast (Sec. 3.6, Table 1).

Statistical hygiene is well above the ICLR norm: bootstrap 95% CIs (10,000 resamples), two-sided sign-flip permutation tests (20,000 permutations), paired d_z, and Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all nine accent-judge tests, with only three cells surviving and this stated plainly (Sec. 4.1).

The decomposition arm avoids the 'difference in significance is a significant difference' fallacy that most papers commit: the authors explicitly test the accent-by-mode interaction (audio vs own transcript = -6.04, 95% CI [-8.5, -3.5], p=4e-4) rather than contrasting p=0.005 with p=0.14 (Sec. 4.2).

Reporting is unusually honest against the authors' own interest: a failed calibration pilot is reported (mean 94.3, SD 4.5 ceiling) along with the redesign it forced (Sec. 3.1); the pre-registered direction-1 prediction is reported as reversed for Nigerian accents (Appendix A); the delivery axis is labelled inconclusive rather than 'no effect' (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 6); and the gold-transcript arm is flagged as a sanity check rather than evidence (Sec. 4.2).

Related work is delineated at a level of precision that is rare — fifteen adjacent papers are each named with the specific reason it does not close the gap (voice-blind judge, test-taker not judge, detect-the-attribute not leak-the-attribute, representational not behavioural), which makes the novelty claim auditable rather than asserted (Sec. 2).

Manipulation checks and exclusion criteria are pre-specified and reported with their failure modes: an 8-clip accent/gender classification check, and a 5%-WER neutrality gate that excluded 5 of 120 delivery conditions, including a candid account of an over-permissive first transcription prompt (Sec. 3.2-3.3).

weaknesses.text: Fatal confound between accent and voice identity: each accent-gender cell is rendered by exactly one TTS voice, so the treatment is not 'accent' but 'this one synthetic voice produced by a natural-language style instruction to gemini-3.1-flash-tts'. The Indian-accent penalty is equally consistent with the TTS engine simply rendering that style prompt with lower fidelity, more artifacts, or lower intelligibility than the American default. With n=1 voice per cell, the accent-level effect has zero degrees of freedom regardless of how many items are averaged, and the 8-clip classifier check establishes only that the accent is recognizable, not that rendering quality is matched. The authors state this limitation (Sec. 5) but the title, abstract, and headline number are all written at the accent-population level the design cannot support.

The rubric explicitly asks the judge to score 'clarity', and clarity is a property of the signal as heard. A judge that lowers a score for a less-intelligible rendering is following the rubric, not exhibiting speaker-identity bias — which makes the 2.50-point audio-mode shift ambiguous between bias and rubric compliance, and would also explain why the effect vanishes under transcript grading (no signal to rate for clarity). The authors identify this exact alternative explanation and name the per-dimension decomposition as the fix (Sec. 5), but do not run it, leaving the bias interpretation of the paper's only significant effect unresolved.

The headline claim rests on one significant cell out of nine (Gemini 3.1 Pro x Indian). The sibling model from the same vendor on the same audio is exactly null (-0.04, p=1.00), the Nigerian direction reverses the pre-registered prediction under both Gemini judges, and the delivery axis is entirely null. The 'three families, three directions' framing reads as a finding, but a single significant cell with an effect of 2.5 points on a 100-point scale, surrounded by nulls and sign reversals, is also fully consistent with one idiosyncratic model-voice interaction rather than a general property of audio-LLM judges.

The third judge family is not a usable judge. The paper itself notes Qwen2-Audio-7B's absolute scores 'cluster on a coarse four-value grid around 75'. A judge that emits ~4 distinct values cannot resolve a 2-point shift, so its positive coefficients (+1.98 to +2.92) are shifts in the rate of quantization-bin flips, not comparable score movements. Building the 'the sign belongs to the judge' claim — one of four stated contributions — on this model is weakly supported.

Scale is far below what the claim requires and below ICLR norms: 24 items, one call per clip, temperature zero, no repeated sampling, no seed variation, a stated $20 compute budget, and per-condition n of 21-48. There is no measurement of judge self-consistency (even at temperature 0, API-served models are not bit-deterministic), so the residual variance attributed to accent is never bounded against judge noise. The authors acknowledge the sample is smaller than the 150-item predecessor design (Sec. 5).

The own-transcript arm is uninterpreted where it is most informative. If the judge's own transcript of the Indian-accented clip contains more recognition errors, the transcript-mode score should fall, not rise by +1.88. No per-accent WER of the judge's own transcripts is reported, so the obvious mediation analysis — does the acoustic penalty track transcription difficulty? — is left undone, and the +1.88 sits unexplained in the middle of the paper's central decomposition.

Zero real speech. Every stimulus is synthetic, and the paper's own related work cites the fragility of TTS-as-stimulus methodology (Yang et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2026). L2-ARCTIC is named as the planned anchor but is blocked on a registration step (Sec. 5). Without any real-speech replication, the finding is about how a Gemini judge reacts to Gemini TTS output — a same-vendor loop the authors also flag for the manipulation check.

Practical consequence is thin relative to the framing. The proposed mitigation — grade from a transcript — is what the majority of deployed ASR-then-LLM assessment pipelines already do, so the paper's actionable output largely confirms an existing default rather than changing practice. A 2.5-point shift on a 100-point scale for one model-accent pair also needs a decision-relevance argument (e.g. effect on pass/fail rates at a realistic threshold) that the paper does not make.

The pre-registration is a commit to the project's own MILESTONES.md rather than a third-party registry, and the paper says so (Appendix A). This is more than most papers offer, but it does not provide the timestamp guarantee the word 'pre-registered' implies in the abstract, and one of the four registered directions is reported as reversed.

The judges are proprietary, versioned, preview-tier endpoints (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-3.6-flash, gemini-3.1-flash-tts-preview). The central result is therefore not reproducible once those endpoints rotate, and the paper offers no open-weight replication of the effect itself — the one open-weight judge shows the opposite sign.

missing_experiment: The same accent contrast with multiple distinct voices per accent-gender cell (five or more, ideally spanning at least two TTS engines) plus a real-recorded-speech replication on L2-ARCTIC. This is the single experiment that separates 'this judge penalizes Indian-accented speech' from 'this judge penalizes one particular synthetic voice', and without it the title claim has n=1 at the level of the treatment. A close second, and much cheaper, is the per-rubric-dimension decomposition (correctness/completeness/helpfulness vs clarity) plus per-accent WER of the judge's own transcripts, which would jointly determine whether the 2.50-point audio-mode penalty is speaker-identity bias or rubric-compliant intelligibility scoring.

format_audit.verdict_vs_norms: Well below ICLR scale norms: 12 pages total (8 of main text) against a median of 25; 6 figures against a mean of 11.5; 2 tables against a mean of 8.7. Table 2's grading-mode decomposition functions as the ablation, and Figure 1 is a proper study-design teaser (page 2 rather than page 1). Error bars and formal significance tests are present throughout, putting the paper above the 40.2% error-bar and 6.1% significance-test rates for accepted ICLR papers — presentation quality and statistical reporting are strengths, but the thinness of tables and appendices reads as a short workshop-style audit rather than a full conference paper, and reviewers will read the low figure/table density as low experimental volume, which here it accurately reflects.

venue_fit.reasoning: Topically this sits comfortably inside ICLR's largest current clusters — LLM-as-judge evaluation, multimodal/audio language models, and LLM safety and fairness — which together account for a large share of the 53.5% LLM-related latest-year output. Stylistically it is a mismatch: ICLR rewards either methodological novelty or large-scale empirical coverage, and this is a small, carefully executed audit with 24 items, three judges, one significant cell, and a $20 compute budget, which reads closer to an Interspeech or ACL-Findings audit paper. The causal framing and clean counterfactual design are the parts that make it plausibly ICLR-shaped; the evidence volume is the part that does not.

calibration_note: Average 4.3 falls in the 4.0-4.5 band, historically ~7.7% accepted at ICLR; at IJCAI/AAAI I would shift one band down (to roughly 3.5-4.0 behaviour, ~2-3%) given their stricter 14-23% overall rates, and the usual caveat applies that a single enthusiastic reviewer or an area chair who values the design's honesty over its scale can move a paper in this range by a full point in either direction.
what_would_move_to_accept: Break the voice-identity confound: re-run Axis A with five or more distinct voices per accent-gender cell across at least two TTS engines, and report the accent effect as a random-effects estimate over voices. This is the difference between a voice-level anecdote and an accent-level claim, and it is the first thing a rigor-focused reviewer will demand. Effort: ~2-3 weeks and a modest compute increase; the pipeline already exists. (highest leverage)

Add the real-speech anchor (L2-ARCTIC or equivalent) so the headline effect is shown at least once on recorded human speech rather than exclusively on synthetic audio from the same vendor as one judge. Effort: 3-4 weeks, mostly gated on the corpus licensing step the paper already reports as pending.

Run the per-rubric-dimension decomposition and the per-accent WER mediation on the judge's own transcripts. Together these determine whether the 2.50-point shift is speaker-identity bias or rubric-compliant clarity scoring, which is currently the strongest alternative explanation for the paper's only significant result. Effort: days, no new stimuli needed.

Scale the item bank from 24 to 150+ and add repeated sampling per clip (5-10 calls) to bound judge self-consistency, then re-report every cell. This would convert the delivery axis from 'inconclusive' to an actual result and would either confirm or dissolve the Nigerian sign reversal. Effort: 1-2 weeks and a compute budget increase of roughly an order of magnitude — still small in absolute terms.

Replace or supplement Qwen2-Audio-7B with an audio judge whose score distribution is not quantized to ~4 values (e.g. a GPT-4o-audio-class model, Qwen2.5-Omni, or an ensemble), so the cross-family sign claim rests on a judge that can actually resolve a 2-point difference. Effort: ~1 week.

Add a decision-relevance analysis: translate the 2.5-point shift into changed outcomes at realistic pass/rank thresholds in the three deployment settings named in the introduction. Effort: 1-2 days, and it converts a small effect size into the practical stake the framing promises.

Expand to ICLR length norms with the additional material this generates — per-item breakdowns, prompt/rubric sensitivity ablations, temperature and ordering ablations, and full appendices of raw distributions per judge. Effort: absorbed by the above.
